>>   Could you also provide the output of the build_env test? It's meant to list relevant information about the test environment for debugging purposes.

> How do I do that? I can't find such test in the cython source.

I think it's just `python3 runtests.py build_env`
Running `CFLAGS="-O1" python runtests.py pycmp_typed` works. So the issue is `-O2` (our default build flags)

> Running `CFLAGS="-O1" python runtests.py pycmp_typed` works. So the issue is `-O2` (our default build flags)

We run them with `-Og` I think (mainly because they run much faster like that). I've tried both `-O2` and `-O3` locally though and failed to reproduce it (although most likely with a different compiler version)

A few experiments:

GCC 16.2.1 and GCC 15.3.0, -O0, -O1, -Og: works
GCC 16.2.1 and GCC 15.3.0, -O2, -O3: fails
clang 22.1.8, any -O: works

I've had a go with `gcc version 16.2.0`, `gcc version 15.2.1`, `gcc version 15.3.0` (the opensuse versions, just because that's what's easiest for me to test. I suspect they aren't completely stock) and haven't been able to make them fail I'm afraid.

Could you please also provide the output of the `build_env` test? Just run `python3 runtests.py build_env`.

~Which C compiler and version are you using?~ From the looks of this, and the lack of other reports so far (there was a long testing phase for this), we should consider a C compiler bug as a reason. ~Could you try a different C compiler version?~

EDIT: Sorry, github hadn't updated my ticket view and I hadn't seen your responses.
So … maybe even an ArchLinux specific patch that broke gcc for this?

I wrote the code that does the comparisons here, so I'm happy to accept bugs on my account, but it's indicative that it's C compiler specific. Apart from a C compiler bug, the second best explanation for optimiser introduced problems in C is usually accidental undefined behaviour, and we have sanitizer checks running that report the test clean, e.g. in https://github.com/cython/cython/actions/runs/32590650966/job/97073860694

After some more testing (not easy becasue it depends independently on CFLAGS and CXXFLAGS, and they seem to be consumed in several different places), to reproduce this you need `-O2` in **CFLAGS** and `-flto=auto` in **CXXFLAGS**:

```
CFLAGS="-O2" CXXFLAGS="-flto=auto" python runtests.py pycmp_typed
```
fails.
```
CFLAGS="-O1" CXXFLAGS="-flto=auto" python runtests.py pycmp_typed
```
works.
```
CFLAGS="-O2" CXXFLAGS="" python runtests.py pycmp_typed
```
also works.
`-flto=auto` reproduces it for me too.

https://github.com/cython/cython/issues/7771 also involved GCC LTO. I'd guess that it might be related (but that's just based on it looking a little similar rather than anything more substantial.

I'll try to have a look at some of the generate failing code for this one later today though, just to convince myself that there's nothing dodgy-looking there.

> I'll try to have a look at some of the generate failing code for this one later today though, just to convince myself that there's nothing dodgy-looking there.

Never hurts to pass a second pair of eyeballs over it. I already did. Some of it feels more dumb than dodgy, but the C compiler should eliminate the redundant parts and make it efficient. I couldn't spot anything suspicious. But I also wrote it, so it might just be author blindness on my side.

and `-fno-ipa-icf` makes it work.

To me this feels like something we're going to need to fix because it's going to keep coming up (even if it's not our fault).

I can't see any way of telling the GCC LTO to ignore a specific function (beyond just surrounding it with general "do not optimize" pragmas, which I don't think we want to do).

I'd imagine the best way might be to make `Eq` the master version (and the define `Ne` in terms of `Eq`) and probably the same thing for `<`/`>=` and `>`/`<=`. That falls apart slight for float and `NaN` though. But possibly only the int versions are causing problems.

The other quicker fix would be to turn of `USE_LONG_INTERNALS` for GCC. That seems to work for me but it's kind of unsatisfactory.
`__attribute__((noipa))` should work here if it's an ICF bug, or even `__attribute__((optimize("no-ipa-icf")))`.

I'll rework the code. ~There is no real reason for separate Python vs. int return variants, so I'll merge those and hopefully fix this issue along the way.~

> There is no real reason for separate Python vs. int return variants

Not entirely true. There is one difference – if we need the `PyObject_RichCompare()` calllback, then we cannot necessarily go through a C `int` return value because the result might be an arbitrary Python object, not limited to `bool`. That's the only reason why I initially wrote it this way.
https://github.com/cython/cython/pull/7919 seems to work.

> [#7919](https://github.com/cython/cython/pull/7919) seems to work.

Works for me too.

I've not had a chance to try reduce anything here, but if you could try get a minimal-ish C testcase, it'd be much appreciated on the GCC side. I can handle the rest if you could share something standalone.

It doesn't need to be elegant or make sense, it just needs to be UB-free and exhibit the problem.
